extracted.intended_audience: conference paper authors (especially junior computing researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and tactical guidelines for writing itemized author responses (conference rebuttals) — typically short (~700 words) responses submitted after reviews to influence program committee discussion and reviewers. Focused on computing conferences but applicable to other venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and timing expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttals are succinct itemized responses, e.g., around 700 words within 4-5 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the rebuttal quickly after reviews (after initial shock) because the author response window is short. Meet with coauthors as soon as possible to devise a rebuttal plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show strong revision competency and commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: For conferences with major revision or conditional accept options, the rebuttal should show the team’s ability and willingness to perform necessary new experiments and revisions within a few months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey realistic plans and timelines for new experiments or fixes; poor rebuttals that fail to demonstrate commitment may indicate low-quality future revisions and reduce chances of acceptance under conditional/major revision tracks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refute factual errors and serious misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the rebuttal to clarify factual errors or serious misunderstandings about novelty, significance, or correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strongly but professionally refute incorrect assertions to set the record straight (important because resubmissions may encounter the same reviewers). Tap into emotional energy but keep the tone factual and evidence-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arm the champion / solidify champion support
rubrics_metrics.description: The rebuttal's strategic mission is to solidify existing champions and provide them with additional evidence so they can better advocate for acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide digestible, persuasive points and evidence a champion can use during discussion. Treat champions’ concerns seriously — weak rebuttals may cause champions to withdraw support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address champions' comments seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume champions' comments are less important; champions expend effort and expect thoughtful responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If champions’ concerns are inadequately resolved, they may stop championing the paper. Ensure you explicitly respond to points a champion raised, with evidence or commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and counter conformity/herd effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize reviewers’ tendency to conform to majority opinions; use the rebuttal to energize discussion and prevent safe convergence to rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize and interpret reviews to highlight fixable issues and persuade borderline reviewers/chairs. PC chairs/area chairs read rebuttals and can ask reviewers whether concerns are addressed — target those decision-makers too.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrase, reorder, and prioritize reviewer comments
rubrics_metrics.description: You control content and order: paraphrase comments in your own words and reorder them by importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing concerns in your words shows understanding. Reordering allows you to lead with the most important points and make the rebuttal easier to follow. Use consistent terminology between question and answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivializing critical questions; provide thoughtful, deep responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical comments require more than a terse yes/no; responses should include evidence, reasoning, and nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brainstorm and share expert insight. Trivializing or shallow answers are a common pitfall. Depth and thoughtfulness help convey technical maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer complex 'Will your solution handle A?' questions with nuanced options
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked whether your solution handles a complex scenario A, do not simply say 'yes' or 'no'; choose from several thoughtful response strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible structured responses include: (1) defend with evidence/reasoning and discuss porting challenges; (2) note the concern is universal and discuss its impact; (3) state it is an open problem and offer insight or planned revision; (4) admit true limitations while explaining possible mitigations; (5) a combination explaining subtleties. Capturing these nuances conveys technical depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide new information rather than repeating the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessively referencing existing sections; the rebuttal is precious space for new content (new data, perspective, or results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include new numbers or experimental data if permitted. Repeating what’s already in the paper is unconvincing and wastes limited rebuttal space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent terminology and clear phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency in terminology between the reviewers’ comments and your responses makes the rebuttal easy to follow and shows understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrase reviewer points using the same or clarified terms, and keep answers concise and directly linked to the paraphrased concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey willingness to revise appropriately for the review track
rubrics_metrics.description: Express a clear willingness to revise, but tailor the level of promised change to the conference’s acceptance options (e.g., major revision vs. conditional accept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may be uncomfortable with conditional accepts if the promised changes imply a drastically different paper. Be specific about what you will change and realistic about scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize the rebuttal to energize reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviews are lukewarm or borderline, the rebuttal should inject clarity and enthusiasm to motivate discussion in your favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret reviews strategically, highlight fixable strengths/novelty, and use tone and organization to deliver some enthusiasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process etiquette: wait, regroup, and plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write a rebuttal in the immediate emotional aftermath of reviews; overcome shock and analyze reviews collaboratively with coauthors before responding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss reviews as a team, plan experiments if needed, and draft a measured, collective rebuttal rather than a reactive single-author reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals are often ineffective for conferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Appealing conference decisions is generally less useful than in journals because new reviewers and existing reviewers may conform to the majority vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than appeal, improve the work and resubmit later. If chairs do solicit more discussion, use the rebuttal to prompt specific questions to reviewers (e.g., 'Does this alleviate your concern?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rebuttals as training for critical thinking and Q&A skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Completing rebuttals improves ability to brainstorm and answer questions clearly, even when acceptance chances are low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat rebuttal writing as practice in concise argumentation and critique response; the exercise has intrinsic professional development value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of the limits of rebuttals — ultimately do strong research
rubrics_metrics.description: A brilliant rebuttal cannot rescue fundamentally ill-formed research; long-term success depends on doing good work first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on strengthening research quality alongside rebuttal tactics; understand that randomness and implicit biases exist in peer review, so persistence and solid research matter most.
